verses.1: Al-Mizan opens the chapter's argument with the universal glorification of God. Dominion belongs wholly to Him, praise belongs to Him because every perfection and beneficence returns to Him, and His power includes every possible thing. These attributes ground what follows: creation, legislation, resurrection, recompense, and the judgment of human belief and disbelief are not outside the sovereignty, knowledge, or power of the One whom all creatures glorify.
verses.2: Al-Mizan reads God created you, then some of you disbelieve and some believe as combining the common origin of humanity with the real distinction introduced by free human response. The verse does not make disbelief a created excuse independent of the human being's act: believers and disbelievers are differentiated in relation to their chosen faith. God's seeing all that they do both records that distinction and prepares for its recompense.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says the heavens and earth were created with truth: their creation is neither play nor falsehood but ordered toward a real end. Human form is made good and proportioned, so bodily creation itself bears a favor and an ordered fitness. The return to God completes this account, for the true creation of a responsible, well-formed human being entails return, judgment, and the manifestation of the end for which that creation was made.
verses.4: Al-Mizan takes divine knowledge of heaven, earth, secrecy, publicity, and the contents of breasts as an ascending clarification: no created realm, public act, concealed act, or inward intention escapes God. What hearts contain is singled out because it is the source from which external deeds arise. The verse thus rules out any thought that hidden disbelief, private intention, or concealed work can evade the Lord who will judge them.
verses.5: Al-Mizan recalls earlier communities who disbelieved and then tasted the evil consequence of their affair. Their history is evidence for the present addressees: denial is not a harmless opinion but an act with a consequence already displayed in the fate of those before them. The painful punishment remains beyond the worldly taste of that consequence, so the report contains both warning from history and warning of the Hereafter.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains the earlier peoples' ruin by their response to messengers who brought clear proofs. They dismissed human messengers as incapable of guidance, confusing the messenger's human nature with an objection to the divine message. Their refusal made them disbelieve and turn away, while God was free of need and Praiseworthy: He does not need their faith, and His sending, command, and recompense remain wise and praiseworthy. The passage rejects readings that make the objection a valid demand for some non-human intermediary; clear proof and divine commissioning are what establish the messenger's office.
verses.7: Al-Mizan treats the deniers' assertion that they will not be raised as a categorical falsehood answered by an equally categorical divine oath. Resurrection is certain; people will then be informed of what they did, and its accomplishment is easy for God. The verse joins the factual certainty of return with the moral purpose of disclosure and recompense, rather than treating resurrection as a bare restoration of bodies.
verses.8: Al-Mizan commands faith in God, His Messenger, and the light sent down with him, the Qur'an, and closes with God's awareness of deeds. Faith in the Messenger is not separable from faith in God because the divine light is received through his mission. Calling the Qur'an light indicates that it brings people out of the darkness of error by showing the true path; the reminder of God's awareness makes obedience to that light an accountable matter rather than an abstract profession.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies the Day of Gathering with the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain. All are gathered so that the real outcome of their transactions becomes visible: the disbeliever loses the happiness and reward for which he was created, while the believer gains them and is spared the evil of his deeds. Faith joined to righteous action is therefore given as the condition for erasing evil deeds and entering gardens beneath which rivers flow, an everlasting success. The verse makes the ultimate loss not a temporary worldly deprivation but the disclosure, on that Day, of what each soul truly gained or forfeited.
verses.10: Al-Mizan contrasts the preceding believers with those who disbelieve and deny the signs. Their residence in the Fire follows from that denial, not from an arbitrary separation, and the verse's closing judgment names it an evil destination.
verses.11: Al-Mizan begins from the principle that no affliction reaches anyone except by God's permission. This does not make affliction purposeless or detach it from human response: whoever believes in God, God guides his heart. The passage explains this guidance as the believer's recognition that the event comes by divine permission, which produces patience and submission rather than revolt; it may also include God's guidance to the consequences of that faith. The verse therefore locates calamity within divine lordship without cancelling responsibility, and ends by grounding both permission and guidance in God's knowledge of all things.
verses.12: Al-Mizan makes obedience to God and obedience to the Messenger the practical demand of the preceding faith. If people turn away, the Messenger bears only clear delivery; their refusal neither creates a defect in his mission nor shifts their burden to him. The distinction preserves both the Messenger's complete discharge of his office and the hearers' responsibility for the response.
verses.13: Al-Mizan reads the exclusive assertion of Godhood as the reason for exclusive reliance. Since no god exists but God, no independent disposer remains in whom believers can place the ultimate trust of their affairs. Tawakkul is therefore not passive abandonment of action but the heart's dependence on the one Lord after recognizing that every effective cause is under His rule.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that some wives and children become enemies when attachment to them draws a believer away from obedience, spending, migration, or another divine duty. The warning is not a command to wrong or abandon them: it requires vigilance against the trial they can present. The verse immediately balances that vigilance with pardoning, overlooking, and forgiving, because the persons may act from weakness or attachment rather than settled enmity and because God Himself is Forgiving and Merciful. The operative point is to prevent family attachment from overcoming loyalty to God while retaining the commanded moral treatment of family.
verses.15: Al-Mizan calls wealth and children a trial because love of them tests whether a person gives precedence to God or to worldly attachment. Their possession is not condemned in itself, but they can become the means of loss described in the prior verse. The great reward with God is set against that unstable test and directs the believer to the proper measure of both.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains fear God as far as you are able as the real limit of obligation, not permission to neglect what one can perform. Hearing, obeying, and spending are named as the concrete form of that capacity, and their good returns to the spenders themselves. The decisive obstacle is the soul's shuhh, an avarice that clings to wealth and resists duty; those protected from it are the successful. Thus the verse joins legal capacity, obedient response, and inner liberation from greed.
verses.17: Al-Mizan takes lending God a good loan as voluntary spending for His cause, described as a loan to honor the giver and guarantee return. God multiplies it and forgives, so the recompense includes both increased reward and removal of fault. His being Appreciative means He acknowledges and amplifies even the servant's small offering, while Forbearing means He does not hasten punishment despite human shortcoming.
